clinician.trajectory_summary: A 7-year-old male with known SLC4A4-related proximal tubular dysfunction underwent superficial keratectomy and presented to the emergency department one day post-operatively with acute onset right-sided body weakness, severe left-sided headache with photophobia and phonophobia, high fever, and altered mental status (irritability, inability to recognize mother, disorientation). Initial physical examination revealed mild distress, irritability, and slight disorientation with intact pupillary responses. Laboratory evaluation on admission showed hypernatremia (150 mEq/L), hypokalemia (3.1 mEq/L), metabolic acidosis (HCO3 17), and elevated urea (90 mg/dl) consistent with his underlying proximal tubular dysfunction, but CRP was normal (0.3 mg/dl). CT brain was unremarkable, excluding acute intracranial pathology such as stroke or hemorrhage. Lumbar puncture with CSF examination was unremarkable, excluding CNS infection. The patient was stabilized with supportive medications and pain management, responded well to treatment, and was discharged home with safety netting. The diagnosis of hemiplegic migraine was established as a diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out structural, infectious, and acute metabolic causes, with the clinical course supporting a migrainous etiology given the complete resolution of neurological deficits with supportive care.
